Let’s explore Chapter 6: The Science of Decomposition—What Nature Teaches Us.
There’s a quiet wisdom in the way nature deals with what’s left behind. You know, for most people, the word “decomposition” instantly brings up images of rot and decay. But in the world of the mortuary, it’s actually seen as something else—a process of transformation.
The mortician often found herself explaining to families that decomposition isn’t something to dread. In fact, it’s nature’s way of recycling—a final act of giving back.
One spring morning, a gardener walked into the funeral home, curious about green burials. She’d spent her life nurturing soil and seeds, and wanted, when the time came, for her own body to help nourish the earth. The mortician gently explained what happens after we die: our cells begin to break down, bacteria and insects join in, and over weeks and months, everything returns to the soil. The gardener listened, and you could see the comfort in her smile—knowing that her last act could be one of renewal.
Most of us don’t realize just how much the environment shapes this process. For example, in a dry, cool place, decomposition slows way down. Sometimes, the body can be preserved for years. But in warmth and moisture, it speeds up, with insects and microbes working together in perfect harmony.
The mortician remembered a family who’d chosen a natural burial in the heart of a forest. Months later, when they visited the site, they expected to find something unsettling. Instead, wildflowers were blooming right where the grave had been. It was clear—death, in its own quiet way, could create something beautiful.
Of course, there are some practical realities to consider. Embalming, refrigeration, and sealed caskets can all slow down decomposition, sometimes for years. People often choose these for cultural or emotional reasons. But here’s something to keep in mind—they can’t stop the process forever.
The mortician once explained to a group of high school students that even in the most high-tech vault, nature eventually finds a way. The students had come expecting scary stories, but left with a new kind of respect—for the quiet persistence of life’s cycles.
Sometimes, families worry about what happens if a body goes undiscovered. The mortician would gently explain that in those cases, decomposition can be quick and dramatic, but it’s never the chaos you see in movies. There’s actually a pattern—a sequence—and even in the messiest situations, there’s a surprising sense of order. Most people, once they understand this, find their fears replaced by a kind of awe.
The science of decomposition reminds us that nothing is ever wasted. Every cell, every molecule, gets repurposed. The mortician saw that for many, knowing this brought a sense of comfort. Death isn’t really an end—it’s a return. It’s a way of joining the endless dance of life and decay.
